title: Global epidemiology and genetic evolution of enterovirus D68 over a decade (2015-24): a systematic review.

analysis.scope_and_question: Enterovirus D68 (EV-D68) is a persistent global health concern, causing mild to severe respiratory disease and, in rare cases, acute flaccid myelitis, a polio-like paralytic syndrome.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: In this systematic review, we synthesised global data on the epidemiology and genetic evolution of EV-D68 from 2015 to 2024 and show its continued widespread circulation and concerning severity.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 8184 EV-D68 cases were reported by 44 countries, and 267 (3·3%) of these cases were EV-D68-associated acute flaccid paralysis cases reported by 26 countries, across all continents. EV-D68 remained associated with severe respiratory disease and acute flaccid myelitis, not only primarily in children younger than five years but also increasingly in adults.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Biennial upsurges followed a distinct every-even-year pattern until 2020, after which the circulation showed geographical diversification in Europe and North America, possibly influenced by the COVID-19 pandemic. Individuals who progressed to acute flaccid paralysis had poor prognosis for full recovery.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Despite limitations in surveillance quality and coverage, the findings underscore the need for sustained surveillance, improved diagnostic strategies, and targeted interventions to mitigate EV-D68-related morbidity.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review examines the global epidemiology and genetic evolution of EV-D68 from 2015 to 2024, highlighting its persistent circulation and association with severe respiratory disease and acute flaccid myelitis. The review reports 8184 cases across 44 countries, with 267 cases of acute flaccid paralysis reported by 26 countries. EV-D68 has been increasingly linked to adults, not just children under five. The biennial pattern of outbreaks shifted after 2020, showing geographical diversification in Europe and North America, possibly due to the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. Individuals with acute flaccid paralysis had poor recovery outcomes. The review emphasizes the need for improved surveillance, diagnostics, and interventions to address the public health burden of EV-D68.

title: Infection-specific long-chain fatty acid metabolism as a broad anti-enterovirus target

analysis.research_question_and_background: Enteroviruses are arguably the most numerous group of viruses infecting humans. While most enterovirus infections are benign and self-resolving, their sheer number inevitably increases the chances of multiple complications.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We explored a shared feature of enterovirus infection, a strong upregulation of phospholipid synthesis in infected cells, as a tool to control enterovirus replication. The study was conducted on diverse enteroviruses in different cell types, including differentiated primary cells.
analysis.methods: The study focused on altering the long-chain fatty acids composition available to infected cells to suppress replication of diverse enteroviruses. The anti-viral activity of LCFAs was assessed in relation to their conformation and not strictly dependent on their degree of unsaturation or capacity to induce lipid peroxidation.
analysis.main_results: The increased phospholipid synthesis consumes endogenously and exogenously derived long-chain fatty acids (LCFA). The inhibition of neutral lipid synthesis promoted LCFAs retargeting to the membranes in infected cells and increased their anti-viral potency.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: We demonstrate that polyunsaturated LCFAs can have a broad anti-enteroviral effect, affecting multiple steps of the virus life cycle. This suggests that their incorporation into the phospholipid molecules makes the replication organelle membranes incapable of properly accommodating viral replication machinery.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: This approach is effective against diverse enteroviruses in different cell types, including differentiated primary cells, and attempts to establish viruses resistant to such treatment were unsuccessful. Targeting infection-induced changes in cellular lipid metabolism may offer a promising approach for controlling enterovirus infections.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The anti-viral activity of LCFAs did not strictly depend on the degree of unsaturation or their capacity to induce lipid peroxidation, but significantly correlated with their conformation. The evidence is strong as the findings were consistent across different cell types and no resistant mutants were successfully selected.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the potential of targeting long-chain fatty acid metabolism as a broad anti-enterovirus strategy. Enteroviruses are the most numerous human viruses, often causing benign infections but also leading to serious complications. The research explores the upregulation of phospholipid synthesis during infection as a universal target for anti-viral interventions. Results show that polyunsaturated long-chain fatty acids (LCFAs) can broadly inhibit enterovirus replication by affecting multiple steps in the virus life cycle, and their anti-viral activity correlates with conformation rather than unsaturation or lipid peroxidation. The study demonstrates that this approach is effective against diverse enteroviruses in various cell types, including differentiated primary cells, and that attempts to develop resistant mutants were unsuccessful. These findings suggest that targeting infection-induced changes in lipid metabolism could offer a promising strategy for controlling enterovirus infections. However, the study's evidence is limited to the conformational properties of LCFAs and does not explore other potential mechanisms or broader implications.

title: Development of Therapeutics for Orthopoxvirus and Enterovirus infections: Small Molecule Antiviral Drug Discovery and Library Generation

analysis.research_question_and_background: Endemic diseases have the potential to spread quickly and overwhelm vulnerable populations, leading to the necessity for antiviral drugs to treat infections. This work focuses on the development of antivirals for orthopoxviruses and enteroviruses, as well as compound library development.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study aimed to develop antivirals for orthopoxviruses and enteroviruses, specifically targeting the p37 protein of poxviruses and the VP1 capsid protein of EV-D68.
analysis.methods: High-throughput screening was used to identify a promising hit molecule for further optimization. The study also developed a direct-to-biology (D2B) methodology to quickly synthesize molecules for screening.
analysis.main_results: Sub-micromolar potency compounds targeting p37 were identified, and Jun14135 and Jun14934 were found to have broad-spectrum antiviral activity against multiple strains of EV-D68.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study identified novel compounds with antiviral activity against poxviruses and EV-D68, which could lead to the development of new treatments for these infections.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings could inform the development of new antivirals for poxviruses and EV-D68, which could improve treatment options and public health responses to these infections.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the use of in vitro models and the need for further in vivo validation. The evidence strength is moderate due to the absence of clinical trial data.

analysis.summary_en: This study developed antivirals for orthopoxviruses and enteroviruses, identifying compounds with sub-micromolar potency against the p37 protein of poxviruses and broad-spectrum activity against multiple strains of EV-D68. The findings could inform the development of new treatments for these infections.
